name: Huaca Pucllana
label: Huaca Pucllana
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Huaca Pucllana' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4966811022: the OpenStreetMap point 'Huaca Pucllana'.
notes: Adobe pyramid of the Lima culture in Miraflores.

text.description:
Huaca Pucllana is a huge stepped pyramid of adobe and clay in the middle of Miraflores, built from seven staggered platforms. It was a ceremonial and administrative centre of the Lima Culture, who lived on the central coast of Peru between about 200 and 700 AD. The enclosure is over 500 metres long, 100 metres wide and 22 metres high. The site museum opened in 1984.

It photographs well because the pyramid is built from rows of small bricks, which catch strong light and throw sharp shadows across the walls. Modern apartment blocks rise right behind it, so you can show an ancient structure inside a busy city. The best-known shot is the pyramid lit up at night, taken from the visitor paths or the restaurant side. Lights and shadows then play across the brickwork.

For the evening shot, arrive around sunset and stay into the evening, before the lights go off. This is about 10:30 pm, but the timing may change. Keep your phone steady against a wall or rail and let it take its time in low light. For a different view, stand on Calle General Borgoño and frame the yellow entrance façade with the site name, the pyramid's adobe face and the street traffic. Check the official site before you go, for entry and photography rules.
text.geographic_location: Huaca Pucllana is in the Miraflores district of central Lima, on General Borgoño (block 8). The pyramid sits right among the apartment blocks and streets of the neighbourhood.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head to General Borgoño (block 8) in Miraflores. The entrance is on that street. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the site itself, so there is no further walk to the subject. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole pyramid with the lights on it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the entrance side to fit in the façade, the adobe wall and the street. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the brick rows and the light and shadow on them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From the site's visitor paths or the restaurant side you can shoot the illuminated pyramid before dinner, with strong light and shadow across the adobe bricks. As an alternative, a second view shows the stepped pyramid in the foreground with Miraflores apartment blocks behind it. Another is from Calle General Borgoño, for the yellow entrance façade with the pyramid's adobe face and street traffic in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the stepped edges of the platforms level with them. Put the pyramid in the lower two-thirds and leave the sky above it. Include a bit of path or wall in front to give a sense of scale. For the street view, line up the yellow façade with the pyramid wall behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone still against a rail or wall until the shot finishes. Tap the brightest part of the pyramid to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the lit bricks don't turn pale.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset and into the evening, before the lights are turned off. This is about 10:30 pm, but it may change.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed archaeological site with its own rules on photography, so check the official site before you go.

name: Larco Museum
label: Larco Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/387071625: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Larco Herrera Museum' (70 m across).

text.description:
The Larco Museum is a privately owned museum of pre-Columbian art in the Pueblo Libre district of Lima. It is housed in an 18th-century vice-royal building, so the setting is as much a part of the picture as the collection. Its galleries give a chronological tour of about 5,000 years of Peruvian history, and it is especially well known for its gallery of pre-Columbian erotic pottery. There is also a Gold and Silver Gallery with crowns, earrings, masks and other ornaments worked in gold.

The collection began in 1925, when Rafael Larco Herrera acquired around 600 ceramic pieces. His son, Rafael Larco Hoyle, built it up, and the museum first opened to the public on 28 July 1926, Peru's Independence Day.

For photographers, the appeal is the mix of old building and carefully lit objects. Outside, step back far enough to take in the building's lines, then move in for details such as doorways, walls and plants. Inside, display cases are the main subject: ceramics and gold ornaments make strong close-ups when you fill the frame with one object. Reflections in the glass are the usual problem, so angle yourself slightly off to one side rather than shooting straight on. Rules on photography inside galleries can differ from room to room, so look out for signs and ask staff if unsure.
text.geographic_location: The Larco Museum is in the Pueblo Libre district of Lima, in an 18th-century vice-royal building.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check a map app for the route to Museo Larco in Pueblo Libre. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of the building and the display cases. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for tight courtyards or to fit more of the façade in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details on ceramics and gold pieces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Frame the exterior from wherever visitors can stand, then go inside for the collection.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight to avoid a leaning look. Outside, fill the frame with one feature such as a doorway or a section of wall. Inside, shoot one object at a time and stand slightly off-centre to the case to avoid your own reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the object to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so gold and bright pieces keep their detail against dark backgrounds. Keep the flash off, as it bounces off glass. Hold the phone steady against your body, since a tripod is unlikely to be allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside, daylight hours give the cleanest views of the building. Inside, lighting is fixed, so time of day matters less; going earlier or at a quieter moment gives you clearer access to the cases.

text.access_note: This is a privately owned museum, so entry is likely to be ticketed and photography rules may apply inside; check the official site before you go.

name: Larcomar
label: Larcomar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Larcomar' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28993402: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Larcomar' (281 m across).
notes: Shopping centre built into the cliff, with ocean views.

text.description: Larcomar is a shopping centre built into the cliff edge in Miraflores, with open-air terraces stepping down towards the Pacific. It photographs well because the whole coastline opens up in front of you: sea, cliffs and, on a clear evening, the sky changing colour above the water. The terrace facing San Lorenzo Island is the classic postcard angle, and from there the frame shows the Pacific coastline, the cliffs and the island. The centre opened on 27 November 1998 and was designed by architect Eduardo Figari Gold. You reach it through Alfredo Salazar Park, which also has a scenic overlook, a children's playground and a few monuments, including a statue of Paddington Bear added in 2015. The terrace is popular, so arrive early if you want a spot at the railing, ideally about an hour before sunset. Start with a wide shot that includes the cliffs and the water, then move in on smaller details: the island, the lines of the cliffs, people at the rail. Keep your lens clean, because sea air can leave a haze on it. If you have time afterwards, Parque del Amor along the coast is a separate sunset photo spot with the El Beso sculpture.
text.geographic_location: Larcomar is in Miraflores District, in Alfredo Salazar Park where José Larco Avenue meets the Malecón de la Reserva. It sits on the cliff edge, directly across the street from the JW Marriott Hotel Lima.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Miraflores and walk or take a taxi to the junction of José Larco Avenue and the Malecón de la Reserva. Walk into Alfredo Salazar Park, which leads to the centre. The phone icon on the map is at Larcomar itself, so once you are inside there is no further walk to the viewpoint. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main terrace view, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more cliff and coastline into the frame. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out San Lorenzo Island or details along the shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the open-air terrace at Larcomar facing San Lorenzo Island and the Pacific. From here the view shows the Pacific coastline, the cliffs and San Lorenzo Island. If the terrace is full, Parque del Amor along the coast is a second option, a separate sunset photo spot with the El Beso sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the top or bottom line so the sea or the sky fills most of the frame. Include a curve of the cliff edge or the terrace railing in the foreground for depth. Keep the horizon level, because it is obvious over open water. Parque del Amor, with the El Beso sculpture, is an alternative if you want a different sunset setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or sea to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. After the sun has gone, try night mode and brace your phone on the railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About an hour before sunset, which also helps you get a place at the railing before it fills up.

text.access_note: The mall has its own access hours and some terraces may be for restaurant customers only at times, so check the official site before you go; the open-air terraces are free to walk into, though a drink or meal is often expected if you want a seat.

name: Parque Kennedy
label: Parque Kennedy
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parque Kennedy' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W194908061 (Parque Kennedy): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Central park of Miraflores, known for its many cats.

text.description:
Parque Kennedy is a city park with flower beds, shade trees and an amphitheatre with curved seating. Pale church towers rise above the greenery. It photographs well because it offers two quite different pictures from one spot: a lively, people-focused scene on the amphitheatre steps, and a calmer view of the church towers framed by leaves and flowers.

The phone icon on the map is inside the park, at the amphitheatre's curved seating. From here the curved steps work as a leading line, drawing the eye into the scene. Visitors and couples often sit on the steps. Small concerts and dancing often happen here too, so the place feels most alive when people gather. If you would rather have a quieter picture, walk a little way off and shoot towards the church towers, using branches and flower beds as a natural frame.

Keep the curve of the steps running diagonally through your frame rather than straight across it. Cats and street performers wander through the park, so you may get a charming extra subject, but nothing is guaranteed in any one place. Be polite when people are in your shot, and ask first if you want a close portrait. Treat the amphitheatre advice as a good starting point and adjust once you see the park for yourself.
text.geographic_location: Parque Kennedy is a city park in Lima, with pale church towers visible rising above the flower beds and shade trees.
text.directions_text: Head for Parque Kennedy in Lima. The phone icon on the map is at the amphitheatre's curved seating inside the park. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for people on the steps. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole curve of the seating. Use the telephoto lens (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the church towers closer over the flower beds.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can photograph visitors and couples on the curved steps. For the alternative, walk to a spot where the pale church towers rise above the flower beds and shade trees, and frame them through the foliage.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and let the curved steps run diagonally from a bottom corner towards the people, so the lines lead the eye into the scene. For the alternative church view, hold the phone so that leaves or branches make a loose frame at the top or the side, with the towers in the gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the people or the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale towers and bright sky keep their detail. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing. Try a Live Photo if there is dancing or music, so you can choose the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evenings, when couples gather and concerts or dancing are more likely.

text.access_note: This is a public park, so check the official site before you go in case of events or restrictions.

name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Lima
label: Lima Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Mayor' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Mayor' (way/24252769): middle (180 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8531715: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Catedral de Lima' (168 m across).
notes: Cathedral on the Plaza Mayor with Pizarro's tomb.

text.description:
Lima's cathedral fills the eastern side of the Plaza Mayor, and its facade, twin bell towers and carved doorways make a solid, symmetrical subject for a phone. The site was once an Inca shrine and the home of an Inca prince. Francisco Pizarro laid the first stone in 1535. The building you see today took its present form between 1602 and 1797, after earthquakes (including a bad one in 1746) forced repeated rebuilding. The current bell towers date from 1794 to 1797. It is described as the oldest and largest church in Peru, and it sits beside the Archbishop's Palace and the Iglesia del Sagrario, so you can often get neighbouring buildings into the frame as well.

The best view is from out in the square, where you can step back far enough to fit the whole front in. Put the central fountain in the foreground and let the colonial palaces on either side frame the cathedral. Keep your phone level so the towers stand straight. If people are crossing the square, wait a moment for a gap, or use them to show the scale of the building. Inside, flash is often banned and some areas may be restricted, so check the signs before you take photos.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Centre of Lima, on the eastern side of the Plaza Mayor, along the second block of Jirón Carabaya. The Archbishop's Palace and the Iglesia del Sagrario stand beside it.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Plaza Mayor in the Historic Centre of Lima. From there the cathedral is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot across the plaza. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole facade, the fountain and the surrounding palaces in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers and the carved doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Mayor (eastern side of the plaza, facing the cathedral front, with the central fountain in the foreground). The cathedral's main facade across the square, framed by the central fountain and the colonial palaces around the plaza. Line up the central fountain in the foreground if it falls between you and the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines. Put the fountain low in the foreground and keep the cathedral in the middle, with a palace on each side. For a quieter alternative, walk to Jirón Carabaya for a side-on view of the cathedral's eastern facade, which is usually less crowded than the middle of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. A Live Photo can help catch a moment with fewer people in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is softer and the square is quieter.

text.access_note: The Plaza Mayor is an open public square, but some areas inside the cathedral may be restricted, so check signage.

name: Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, Lima
label: San Francisco Convent
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza San Francisco' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/435365880: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Monastery of San Francisco' (189 m across).
notes: Yellow baroque convent famous for its catacombs and library.

text.description: The Basilica and Convent of San Francisco is a large Franciscan complex in the Historic Centre of Lima, which UNESCO added to its World Heritage List in 1991. The part most visitors photograph is the Baroque church facade, with its twin towers and rhythmic stonework, set behind an open square. Lima was founded in 1535, and the Franciscans were given land in the new city soon after. An earthquake in February 1655 brought the first convent down. The first stone of the rebuilt convent was laid in May 1657, and it was inaugurated in October 1672. Inside, the cloisters have Sevillian tile plinths and cedarwood ceilings. The church was raised to the rank of minor basilica in 1963. For a phone photo, the facade works because it is one clear, symmetrical subject with plenty of space in front. The subject sits at the centre of the convent complex, not in front of the church, so do not treat it as the place to take the facade photo. The place for the facade is Plaza San Francisco in front of the entrance, if it is open. The cloisters are a good second subject, with arcades and tilework, but they are inside the convent. Rules on photography inside the church and convent seem to vary, so look for posted signs. The square in front has had access restrictions in recent years because of works and a dispute over the space, and it has been reported closed to the public since August 2022, so check the current situation before you plan your visit around it.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Centre of Lima, in a block bounded by Amazonas, Áncash and Lampa streets and Abancay Avenue. The Baroque church sits beside the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Solitude and the Church of the Virgin of the Miracle.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Historic Centre of Lima by taxi or on foot and ask for the Basilica and Convent of San Francisco. The complex lies between Áncash, Lampa and Amazonas streets and Abancay Avenue. Once there, walk to the front of the church. The subject is at the centre of the complex, and the plaza viewpoint may be closed, so check access. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole facade and its two towers. If you cannot get far enough back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the towers do not lean inwards. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tops of the towers and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is at the centre of the convent complex. For the facade shot, stand in Plaza San Francisco in front of the entrance, if access is open. From there you see the yellow Baroque facade with its twin towers, framed by the open stone square in front of the entrance. If you go inside the convent, the cloisters give a different view of arcaded courtyards and tilework, with the bell tower visible from the cloisters.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the facade with the middle of the frame so both towers look balanced. Keep a strip of the square at the bottom to give a sense of scale. Then step closer and use zoom for a tighter shot of the towers or doorway. If you visit the cloisters, shoot along an arcade to catch the tilework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the yellow walls keep their colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a couple of frames in case one is soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is not directly behind the facade, as it can turn the front dark. Early or later in the day usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows.

text.access_note: The church and convent are a ticketed visit and the square in front has had restricted access in recent years, and has been reported closed to the public since August 2022, so check the official site before you go and look for signs about photography inside.

sources.title: Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, Lima

name: Lima Art Museum
label: Lima Art Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6033913: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Main art museum in the Palacio de la Exposición.

text.description:
The Lima Art Museum, known as MALI, sits in the Palacio de la Exposición, a grand building at the edge of Exposition Park, close to the entrance to Lima's historic centre. It was built for the 1872 World's Fair. Its Italianate façade was designed by Antonio Leonardi, an Italian architect living in Lima, and wraps around an iron structure that came from Gustave Eiffel's workshop in 1870-71. The museum itself opened in 1961, and its collection covers almost 3,000 years of Peruvian art, from the pre-Columbian period to today.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the palace itself: a long, symmetrical, classical Italianate frontage. The building is wide, so you will need to step back as far as the space allows to fit it in. Look for the centre line of the façade and use your phone's gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Check what the surroundings look like when you arrive, and if anything sits at the edge of the frame, make sure it does not cover the building's details.

The park once housed other structures, including the Moorish and Byzantine pavilions built in 1921 for Peru's centennial of independence. Check what is visible when you arrive, as they may make good extra pictures if you have time to look around. If you want to photograph inside the museum, check the official site before you go, as access and photography rules may vary.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Lima, in Exposition Park next to the entrance to the historic centre. The museum occupies the Palacio de la Exposición.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the historic centre of Lima, which is right next to the park. From there, head towards Exposition Park and look for the large palace at its edge. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi and ask for the Museo de Arte de Lima (MALI). The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close to the façade, since the building is very wide. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view with less stretching at the edges. If you can see decorative details higher up, a telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) will pick them out.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then step back as far as the space allows to find a view that fits the full width of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the building with the middle of the frame so the symmetry shows. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean. If you can, include a little of the ground in front of the building to give a sense of scale. For a different shot, move in with the telephoto and photograph a section of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its colour and detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, when the façade is evenly lit, is the easiest for a clear shot. Early or late in the day can give softer light, but check where the sun falls on the building first.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for current access conditions, both for the museum and for the surrounding park. The museum is a ticketed site.

name: Plaza San Martín, Lima
label: Plaza San Martín
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jirón de la Unión' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jirón de la Unión nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/44364378: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'San Martin Park' (219 m across).
notes: Grand square with the monument to San Martín.

text.description: Plaza San Martín is one of the most representative public squares in Lima, set in the Historic Centre, which UNESCO made a World Heritage Site in 1988. It was opened on 27 July 1921 to mark 100 years of Peruvian independence. The Spanish architect Manuel Piqueras Cotolí designed the layout, and the central monument to the liberator José de San Martín is by the sculptor Mariano Benlliure. The plaza photographs well because the buildings around it were put up in stages between 1914 and 1945, yet they share a similar neocolonial look. That gives you a tidy, even backdrop. The Hotel Bolívar (1924) and the Zela and Pumacahua arcades (1926) are two of the best-known parts of the frame. The best first shot is from the end of Jirón de la Unión, the pedestrian street that links the plaza with the Plaza Mayor. From there the street's facades and passing shoppers lead your eye towards the plaza's grand buildings. Once you are in the square, turn to the bronze statue of San Martín with the facades behind it. The arcades are good for a calmer, shadier picture with columns and shopfronts. Go in the morning if you can, when the light reaches down the street before the coastal mist (garúa) settles. Keep your phone level so the tall buildings do not lean inwards, and wait a moment for a gap in the crowd.
text.geographic_location: Plaza San Martín is in the Historic Centre of Lima, at the ninth block of Avenida Colmena. It is a short walk from the Plaza Mayor, to which it is linked by the pedestrian street Jirón de la Unión.
text.directions_text: Head for the Historic Centre of Lima and look for Plaza San Martín. On foot, the pedestrian street Jirón de la Unión links the Plaza Mayor with the plaza, so you can walk down it and start your photos at the plaza end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view, as it keeps the buildings looking natural. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the square itself to fit the statue and the surrounding facades into one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the statue or the arcade columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jirón de la Unión (the end of the pedestrian street nearest the plaza, looking back toward the Plaza de Armas). A framed view of the plaza's monumental buildings at the end of the pedestrian street, with the street's facades and shoppers leading the eye in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street's building edges up with the vertical lines, so the street forms a frame around the plaza buildings. Let people walking in the street fill the foreground for a sense of life and scale. For a second view, go into Plaza San Martín to photograph the bronze statue of General San Martín with the facades around it. Or shoot from the Portales de Zela y Pumacahua, where the columns and shopfronts make a shaded, more intimate composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest building facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and pale stonework keep their detail. If a Live Photo is on, it can catch the movement of people in the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before the garúa (coastal mist) settles, when the light reaches down into the street.

text.access_note: Plaza San Martín is a public square and Jirón de la Unión is a pedestrian street, but check the official site before you go for any events or restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Plaza San Martín and Jirón de la Unión are normally open public spaces with no entry ticket.
The pedestrian street is likely to be busier with people at midday than in the early morning.
Keeping the phone level reduces the look of buildings leaning inwards.

name: Plaza Mayor, Lima
label: Plaza Mayor
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palacio de Gobierno' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Palacio de Gobierno' (relation/8052132): middle (237 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/172097116: 'Goddess Feme', the best-known feature inside 'Main Square of Lima' (195 m across).
notes: The historic main square of Lima.

text.description:
The Plaza Mayor, also called the Plaza de Armas, is the main square of Lima's historic centre. It goes back to the city's foundation by Francisco Pizarro on 18 January 1535. Around it stand the Government Palace, the Metropolitan Cathedral, the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace. In 1821 José de San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence here. The fountain in the middle was inaugurated on 8 September 1651 and is still the centrepiece.

From here you can frame the ornate front of the presidential palace, which was completed in 1938, with the open square and a guard in the foreground. Looking south-west across the square, you see the central part of the plaza and the Goddess Feme feature, about 160 m away. Late afternoon is a good time, as the light is warmer and the changing of the guard takes place then.

For variety, try one wide shot of the whole square with the Cathedral, the palace and the fountain. Then take a quieter detail shot of the carved balconies of the Archbishop's Palace on the square's edge, from the street. Keep your phone ready for the guards, and expect other visitors to wander through your frame.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Lima, the main square bounded by Carabaya, Junín, Huallaga and Unión streets. The Government Palace and the Metropolitan Cathedral stand on its sides.
text.directions_text: Head for the historic centre of Lima and ask for the Plaza Mayor (also called the Plaza de Armas). From there, the Goddess Feme feature is about 160 m to the south-west, a short walk across the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the palace front and the square in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the guard with the facade behind. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved and decorated details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Palacio de Gobierno (front facade facing the Plaza Mayor). The ornate main façade of the presidential palace, ideally framed with the square and a guard in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the palace's vertical lines straight. Put the guard or a few people in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different view, take a wide shot of the whole square with the Cathedral, the palace and the fountain. Or take a close detail of the Archbishop's Palace balconies from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace front to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the stonework. Hold your phone steady, and try a Live Photo for the guard.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is warm and the guard change usually takes place. Times can vary, so check on the day.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but parts of it can be closed for security operations, events or barriers, and photography inside the Cathedral and the government buildings may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
general_tips: Ultra-wide lenses can stretch or bend buildings near the edges of the frame, so keep the palace away from the very edge.
Other visitors are likely to pass through the foreground at busy times.

name: Government Palace, Peru
label: Government Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Mayor' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Mayor' (way/24252769): middle (180 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8052132: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Goverment Palace' (237 m across).
notes: Presidential palace, with a changing of the guard at noon.

text.description: The Government Palace is where Peru's president works and lives, and it takes up the northern side of Lima's Plaza Mayor. Francisco Pizarro built the first palace on this spot in 1535. Fires in 1884 and 1921 destroyed much of the later building, and what you see today was built between 1926 and 1938. The facade facing the square was designed by the Polish architect Ricardo de Jaxa Malachowski and is inspired by the Neo-Baroque style. It is a long, formal front with plenty of detail, which makes it a good subject for a phone. The square also gives you a lot to work with. The bronze fountain makes a natural foreground, and the colonial buildings around the plaza frame the palace from the side. Ceremonial guard units are stationed at the palace and take part in a daily Changing of the Guard. The guards in red dress uniform give you a moving subject, though the noon ceremony draws a crowd, so expect to wait for a clear view. The palace interior is not open to independent visitors, so all your pictures will be taken from outside. Take one wide shot to show the whole building with the fountain, then a few closer ones of the guards and the facade detail. Keep the phone level so the long horizontal lines stay straight.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Lima, on the northern side of the Plaza Mayor (also called the Plaza de Armas), with the Rímac River just behind the palace.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Plaza Mayor in Lima's historic centre. Walk towards the palace front and stop once the whole facade fits in your screen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, the palace and the buildings around the plaza in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the facade. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the guards and the architectural detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Mayor (central bronze fountain, looking toward the palace facade on the east side of the square). The palace's neo-baroque facade across the square, framed by the bronze fountain in the foreground and the colonial buildings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain in the lower part of the frame, with the palace facade filling the middle. Keep the phone level so the building's lines stay straight. For a different view, try a wider, calmer shot of the palace and the surrounding colonial architecture before the tour groups arrive. When the guards are marching, switch to telephoto and photograph the red uniforms against the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. For the guards, try Live Photos or a burst so you can pick the best moment from the march.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when warm light falls on the yellow colonial facades around the plaza. For fewer people in the frame, go early, before tour groups arrive.

text.access_note: You photograph the palace from the open square outside; the interior is not open to independent visitors, so check the official site before you go.

name: Circuito Mágico del Agua
label: Magic Water Circuit
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fuente Mágica' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fuente Mágica' (way/129490574): middle (75 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM N1432367035 (Circuito Mágico del Agua): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Park of illuminated fountains, best seen at night.

text.description:
The Circuito Mágico del Agua is a park of illuminated fountains inside Parque de la Reserva in Lima. For a phone photo, the Fuente Mágica is the easiest place to start. Its tall central jet rises in front of the neoclassical arches of the Logia colonnade, which gives you a ready-made park panorama with the water in the foreground and the arches as a backdrop. The Logia is one of the park's notable architectural features, and its repeating arches make a tidy frame for the jet.

There are two other subjects worth knowing about. The Fantasy Fountain throws up a water screen about 120 metres wide. During the evening show, jets and laser light form images against the water. The Catarata de Pumawasi is a cascade of roughly 12 metres. It is lit by daylight, so it makes a calmer daytime picture away from the evening crowds.

For practical photo advice, show times vary by season and day, so check the schedule on the day. Arrive early if you want a front spot at the evening show. Keep your phone's lens clean, because spray and fingerprints soften night shots quickly. One guide says photography is allowed for non-commercial use, but check the park's rules before you go. Move around the fountain a little before you settle on a view, as small steps left or right change how the arches line up behind the jet.
text.geographic_location: The circuit is inside Parque de la Reserva in Lima. The Fuente Mágica, with the Logia colonnade behind it, is a classic view of the park.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to find a route to Parque de la Reserva. Walk south-west from it to reach them. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the jet with the Logia arches behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole colonnade in, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Pumawasi cascade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (view with the Logia colonnade behind the fountain). The Magic Fountain's tall jet framed by the neoclassical arches of the Logia monument, a classic park panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the jet on a vertical line, so the arches sit evenly on both sides. Keep the horizon level, because the colonnade makes any tilt obvious. If you want a different picture, the Fantasy Fountain's water screen is the show-night alternative, and the Pumawasi cascade is a quieter daytime one.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the jet to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit water does not turn white. For the evening show use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The Fantasy Fountain show is in the evening, while the Pumawasi cascade is better in daylight. Show times vary by season and day, so check the official schedule and arrive early for the front spots.

text.access_note: The park needs an entrance ticket, and show times and prices change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Spray and fingerprints on the phone lens can soften night shots.

name: Chinese Arch, Lima
label: Barrio Chino Arch
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arco Chino' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Jirón Ucayali and Jirón Andahuaylas (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/317232859: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chinatown Gate' (15 m across).

text.description:
The Chinese Arch (Arco Chino) is a paifang, a traditional Chinese-style gateway, and it marks the entrance to Lima's Chinatown in Barrios Altos. It was a gift from Lima's Chinese community, together with the government of Taiwan, to mark 150 years of Peruvian independence, and it was inaugurated on 12 November 1971. It stands 8 metres high and 13 metres wide, with a wood-and-marble covering decorated by the artist Wa Kong Chang. Two guardian lion sculptures, each 1.80 metres tall, were unveiled in 2017.

It photographs well because it is bold, red and gold, and very symmetrical. The most popular picture is the straight-on view from the Calle Capón side, with the lions on either side and the arch centred in the frame. The lintel carries Chinese characters. On the Calle Capón side it reads 'Under the same sky, we are all equal', which is a nice detail to catch if you zoom in a little.

Go early in the morning if you can, as the area is busy through the day and the street is uneven underfoot, so watch your step while you line up your shot. For a second picture, walk onto pedestrian Calle Capón and shoot back so the arch sits in the foreground with the street stretching away behind it. That gives a better sense of the depth of the neighbourhood.
text.geographic_location: The arch is in Barrios Altos, in central Lima, at the entrance to Chinatown where Jirón Ucayali meets Jirón Andahuaylas, beside the start of pedestrian Calle Capón.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Barrios Altos and ask locally for the Arco Chino or Calle Capón. Once you are on Calle Capón, the arch is hard to miss. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on, symmetrical view. If the crowds force you to stand close, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole gateway in. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the lions and the characters on the lintel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Jirón Ucayali and Jirón Andahuaylas (Stand straight in front of the Calle Capón face of the arch). A centred, symmetrical view of the red and gold gateway, with its guardian lions on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the middle of the arch on the centre line so both lions balance. Keep your phone level, as tilting will make the gateway look lopsided. For a second picture, move onto Calle Capón and shoot back so the arch is in the foreground and the pedestrian street runs away behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the red and gold stay rich rather than washed out against the sky. Try a short Live Photo to catch passers-by moving through the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the crowds are thinner and it is easier to get a clear frontal shot.

text.access_note: The arch stands at a street entrance to Chinatown and there is no charge to photograph it, though the street can be busy and uneven, so take care.

name: Palacio de Torre Tagle
label: Torre Tagle Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palacio de Torre Tagle patio' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4486063699: the OpenStreetMap point 'Palacio Torre Tagle'.
notes: Baroque mansion known for its carved balconies.

text.description:
Palacio de Torre Tagle is a colonial mansion in the historic centre of Lima, finished in 1735 for José Bernardo de Tagle Bracho, the first Marquis of Torre Tagle. It later became part of Peru's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is why the inside is not a normal open-door museum. The building covers about 1,699 square metres, and its stone portal and two carved cedar-and-mahogany balconies are among the best-known colonial façade details in the city. The right-hand balcony has three sections and the left-hand one has seven, so the front looks pleasingly lopsided.

The part most visitors can hope to see is the central courtyard. It is open to the sky and surrounded by two levels of galleries, with stairways, black-and-white floor tiles, a central statue and a carved lion. That mix of repeating arches, patterned floor and warm wood gives a phone plenty to work with, and you do not need to wait for a clear view because the space is enclosed. Try a straight-on shot down the middle, then a second one angled along a gallery so the arches lead the eye.

If the courtyard is closed when you arrive, the street view still works. Step back on Jirón Ucayali and photograph the portal and balconies among the neighbouring colonial façades. Access can change, so check current access before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Lima, on Jirón Ucayali, about two blocks southeast of the Plaza Mayor.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so start from the Plaza Mayor and walk southeast along Jirón Ucayali. The palace is about two blocks southeast of the Plaza Mayor, and its stone portal and wooden balconies are easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole two-level courtyard, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the galleries. Switch to 2x or the telephoto for carved details such as the lion, the balcony woodwork and the tiles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look across the open two-level galleries to the stairways, the black-and-white floor tiles, the central statue and the carved lion. If the patio is closed, the alternative is Jirón Ucayali outside, for the stone portal and the two carved balconies.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the gallery columns with the vertical lines so the arches look straight. Put the tiled floor in the lower third as a leading pattern. Wait a moment for people to move out of the middle if you can. For a second picture, include the statue or the lion in the foreground and let the galleries sit behind it. From Jirón Ucayali, stand back far enough to fit both balconies in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brighter gallery walls to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or sunlit stone looks washed out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, since the shaded galleries may be dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is best, because the courtyard is open to the sky. Visiting times for the courtyard can vary, so check current access first.

text.access_note: The palace is a working government building and the interior is restricted, with visits limited to the courtyard at most, so check current access before you go.

name: Casa de Aliaga
label: Casa de Aliaga
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Mayor de Lima' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Mayor de Lima' (way/172097116): middle (195 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8607870: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (94 m across).
notes: Oldest colonial mansion in Lima, still family-owned.

text.description:
Casa de Aliaga is a colonial house in the historic centre of Lima. It stands on a huaca (a pre-Hispanic sacred site) and dates back to May 1536, the first years of Lima's founding. It was built for the conquistador Geronimo de Aliaga. The same family is said to have lived in it for seventeen generations over five centuries. After the 1746 earthquake destroyed it, the house was rebuilt, and further work followed in the 19th century. That explains its mix of architectural styles.

From the street it looks fairly plain, so the photo to aim for is the dark carved wooden balconies against the lighter façade, shot looking up from below. For a wider picture of the setting, start on Plaza Mayor de Lima, which is only a short walk away. From there you can fit the fountain, the palm trees and the colonial façades of the cathedral and government palace into one frame. The house is a short walk to the north, so it will not be in that shot. Treat the plaza as the scene-setter and the street as the close-up.

If you want to photograph inside, such as the courtyard, chapel or rooms, you need a guided visit booked in advance, and flash is not allowed. Check the official site before you go. Outside, take your time: the balconies reward a slightly closer look, and the street is the easiest place to get them clean.
text.geographic_location: Casa de Aliaga is in the historic centre of Lima, a short walk north of Plaza Mayor de Lima, which has the cathedral and the government palace on its sides.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot; head to the historic centre and walk to Plaza Mayor de Lima. Stand there first. From the plaza, Casa de Aliaga is to the north, about 3 minutes on foot. Walk slowly along the street and look up to find the balconies. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the plaza to fit in the fountain, palms and façades. Use the default lens (1x) for the street view of the house. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the balconies from across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Mayor de Lima. A wide view across the plaza with the fountain, palm trees and colonial façades of the cathedral and government palace, with the Casa de Aliaga a short walk away. It is not in this view, so this is the setting shot. For the house itself, walk to the street in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: On the plaza, turn on gridlines and place the fountain in the lower part of the frame, with the cathedral façade and palms behind it. At the house, stand close to the wall and angle the phone upward so the dark carved wooden balconies sit against the lighter façade. Keep the phone level, tilting only slightly, so the building does not lean too much.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the balconies to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the dark wood keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides suggest sunset for the plaza, when the light is golden and the shadows are long. The street in front of the house is easiest when the light falls on the balconies rather than behind them.

text.access_note: The plaza and the street outside are open public space, but going inside the house needs a guided visit booked in advance, so check the official site before you go.

name: Plaza de toros de Acho
label: Plaza de Acho
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cerro San Cristóbal' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cerro San Cristóbal' (node/3089912523): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1932068250: the OpenStreetMap point 'Plaza de Toros de Acho'.
notes: One of the oldest bullrings in the Americas.

text.description:
The Plaza de Toros de Acho is Lima's main bullring, a round arena on the edge of the historical centre in the Rímac district. It is a national historic monument and opened on 30 January 1766. That makes it the oldest bullring in the Americas and the second-oldest in the world, after La Maestranza in Spain. It holds 13,700 people and was built of adobe and wood. The land was once called "el Hacho", a Quechua word for an elevated place with a view, which is a nice fit for the photo suggested here.

The best-known picture is from above. From the summit lookout on Cerro San Cristóbal, the recommended elevated viewpoint, you look down on the circular red ring, with the Rímac river and the historic centre of Lima beyond it. From up there the shape of the ring is easy to read, which is hard to do from the street. Cerro San Cristóbal is the viewpoint, and the two are not the same place.

If you want a ground-level shot as well, the exterior and entrance seen from the street make a good second picture of the monument. Bullfights are held on Sundays through October and November, during the Señor de los Milagros fair, so the arena may be closed to visitors at other times. Check the official site before you go. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, so you have both the wide scene and a close shot of the ring.
text.geographic_location: The bullring is in the Rímac district, beside the historical centre of Lima.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are nearby, so start from the Rímac district beside Lima's historical centre. Check how to get to the summit lookout on Cerro San Cristóbal before you go. For the ground-level view, ask a taxi driver to take you to the Plaza de Toros de Acho in Rímac. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the ring, the river and the city beyond. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the bullring closer and fill the frame with its circular shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cerro San Cristóbal (summit lookout over the bullring). An elevated view looking down on the circular red bullring, with the Rímac river and the historic center of Lima beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the ring in the lower or middle part of the frame, with the river and the centre of Lima behind it as context. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. For a different picture, go to the street entrance and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the exterior and doorway, which is the ground-level view of the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bullring to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright and washing out the colours. Panorama mode can capture the whole sweep of the city from the lookout. Hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear part of the day when the city is not hazy, so the ring and the centre beyond it stay sharp.

text.access_note: Check access to the hill lookout before you go. The bullring's interior may have access limits and may be closed outside the Sunday bullfight season in October and November, so check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica and Convent of Santo Domingo, Lima
label: Santo Domingo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plazuela de Santo Domingo' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Museo Convento de Santo Domingo' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5722131: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colonial convent with a tiled cloister.

text.description:
The Basilica and Convent of Santo Domingo is a religious complex created in the 1530s, when the city was newly founded. It took about 50 years to build. Earthquakes destroyed the first church in 1678, and later quakes forced more rebuilding, so what you see today is a layered result. The church became a Minor Basilica in 1930. It holds the relics of Rose of Lima and Martin de Porres, and the University of San Marcos began teaching here in the 16th century.

The best-known feature from outside is the bell tower. It was designed in 1766 in the Rococo style, stands 46 metres high, and is topped by a figure of an angel with a trumpet. The base still shows the rough, blocky stonework that once covered the first church's front.

For a phone photo, the small plaza in front of the church works well. You can frame the church front with the old carved wooden balconies of the neighbouring houses around it, which gives a sense of the historic centre rather than just a building. Stand back, keep your phone level, and use the gridlines to keep the tower upright. Zoom in for the angel and the upper tower. If you want a view over the convent roofs and dome, the bell tower is an alternative, but it needs a ticket and a guided visit, so check current ticket details and opening hours before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Centre of Lima, on the small plaza that fronts the church.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Historic Centre of Lima and the Plazuela de Santo Domingo. Once the church is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. Walk towards the church front and the bell tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the church front and the balconies around the plaza. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the bell tower and its trumpet-bearing angel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plazuela de Santo Domingo. The church front opening onto the small plaza, with old carved wooden balconies on the neighbouring houses in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the church front in the centre and let a balcony fill one side of the frame to give depth. Turn on the gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so it does not lean. For a different view, the convent's bell tower looks over the roofs and dome towards the historic centre, but it needs a ticket and a guided visit.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white and pink tower does not wash out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or times when the light falls from the side suit the main front best, because it brings out the carving and the texture of the walls.

text.access_note: The plaza in front is an open public square, but the church is a place of worship and the cloister and bell tower need a ticket and guided visit, so check current ticket details and opening hours before you go.

name: Palacio Municipal de Lima
label: Municipal Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Mayor' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Mayor' (way/24252769): middle (180 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5200998: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: City hall on the Plaza Mayor.

text.description: The Municipal Palace is the seat of the Metropolitan Municipality of Lima, and it stands right beside the Plaza Mayor in the Historic Centre. Its bright yellow facade, wooden balconies and arcade make it one of the easiest buildings on the square to photograph. The plaza gives you plenty of open ground to step back and fit the whole front into one frame. The town council has been on this site since 1548, when it moved to land that had belonged to Hernando Pizarro. The first council building was fairly plain, and the 1746 Lima-Callao earthquake destroyed about 90% of the city's colonial civil buildings. What you see today is therefore a later story than the early council houses. For a good photo, stand out in the plaza and let the yellow wall fill the frame, with the balconies running across it. People walking through the square add scale and life to the picture. If you want something less crowded, the side passage and side street next to the palace give a closer, angled view of the wall and balconies. Check for any closures around the square before you set up, as the area around a government building can be restricted at times.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Centre of Lima, on the third block of Jirón de la Unión, right next to the Plaza Mayor (also called Plaza de Armas).
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed nearby, so head on foot or by your usual local transport to the Plaza Mayor in the Historic Centre of Lima. From there the palace is about 95 m to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the plaza to take in the whole yellow facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move close to the palace in the side passage and want to fit the wall and balconies in. Use 2x or more, if your phone has it, to pick out the balconies and arcade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Mayor (from the central fountain or the plaza's open ground, facing the palace on the west side). The yellow facade of the Municipal Palace with its wooden balconies and arcade, framed across the open plaza. Face north-west towards the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the arcade up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Keep the fountain or some open plaza in the foreground for depth. For a closer, angled shot of the side wall and balconies, try the passage called Pasaje Santa Rosa beside the building. The street Jirón Conde de Superunda shows the side of the palace and its balconies with fewer people around.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the yellow stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Turn on Live Photos if people are crossing the square, so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer light is usually found early or late in the day, but the facade is easy to photograph at most times of day.

text.access_note: The Plaza Mayor is an open public square, but the palace is a government building and security closures may apply, so check the official site before you go.

name: Archbishop's Palace, Lima
label: Archbishop's Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Mayor' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Mayor' (way/24252769): middle (180 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/435559310: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo del Palacio Arzobispal de Lima' (69 m across).
notes: Ornate carved wooden balconies next to the cathedral.

text.description:
The Archbishop's Palace is the home of the Archbishop of Lima and the administrative headquarters of the Archdiocese. It stands on the east side of the Plaza Mayor, right beside the cathedral. The land was set aside for Lima's head priest by Francisco Pizarro after the city was founded in 1535. The building you see today is much newer: it opened on 8 December 1924 and is a good example of Spanish Colonial Revival style. Its architect, Ricardo de Jaxa Malachowski, took the Torre Tagle Palace as a reference.

It photographs well because the pale front is full of detail without being cluttered. Ornate cedar balconies sit over the main doors, and a granite statue of Saint Turibius of Mongrovejo, patron protector of the Archdiocese, tops the building. Two flagpoles, for the Peruvian and Vatican flags, add a little colour. The view from across the open square lets you take in the whole facade with the cathedral alongside, which is how guides suggest studying it.

Start with a wide shot of the full front, then move in on the balconies and the statue. The square is open, so you can step back and forth to adjust your framing. Inside, the palace is a museum with a grand staircase and stained glass, but rules on photography and entry can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Historic Centre of Lima, on the east side of the Plaza Mayor (also called Plaza de Armas), directly next to Lima Cathedral.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Plaza Mayor in the Historic Centre of Lima. Once you are in the square, the palace is on the east side, next to the cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the cathedral beside it. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the front. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved balconies and the statue on the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Mayor (from the open plaza, looking at the palace's facade on the square's east side, next to the cathedral). The palace's pale neo-colonial front with its large carved wooden balconies, seen across the square and alongside Lima Cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with them so the walls don't lean. Take one wide shot with the cathedral beside the palace, then a tighter shot of the balconies. Keep a little open square in the foreground for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale stonework keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon is likely to be kinder to the facade, because it faces across the square to the west. Early in the day, the front may be more in shade.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the open square; the museum inside may have its own entry and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica and Convent of Nuestra Señora de la Merced
label: La Merced Church
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q4867359: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Baroque church with an elaborate carved façade.

text.description: La Merced is one of the oldest churches in Lima, and its carved stone front is the reason to stop here. The entrance is packed with detail, with a statue of the Virgin of Mercy in a central niche and other figures around her. The Baroque style is the Lima version known as Churrigueresque. The church and convent are as old as the city itself. The current stone entrance dates from 1696, and the tower, staircase and interior balconies were rebuilt between 1759 and 1762 after earthquake damage. Early in the 20th century the front was covered in thick plaster in a French-looking style, and that was removed in 1940, so you now see the original face of the building. The church stands on Jirón de la Unión, in the historic centre, at the corner with Jirón Antonio Miró Quesada. For a phone photo this means a busy street scene with a richly carved front, so the main task is to keep the building upright and fit in as much of the entrance as you can. The phone icon on the map is only a few steps from the church, which helps in a narrow street. Take one wide shot to show the church in its setting, then a closer shot of the carved entrance and the central niche. Interiors and the cloisters may have their own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Lima, on Jirón de la Unión at the corner with Jirón Antonio Miró Quesada.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or stop is listed for this spot, so head for Jirón de la Unión 621, at the corner with Jirón Antonio Miró Quesada, in the historic centre. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi to the historic centre. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) because the street is narrow and the church is tall. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the front. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the carved entrance and the statue in its niche.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the tower and entrance with them. Keep the phone level, because tilting it up makes the building lean backwards. Leave some space around the church to show the street, then step in or zoom for a second shot of the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the carved stonework to focus and pull the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the detail in the stone does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning, when the street is quieter, is usually easiest for a clear view of the front.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship and may have set visiting times and dress expectations, so check the official site before you go.
